learningObjective: Distinguish `torch.cond` from `torch.where` and identify when each is the appropriate rewrite for a data-dependent branch.
stem: You have a data-dependent branch on a tensor value that causes a graph break. When choosing between `torch.where(cond, a, b)` and `torch.cond(cond, fn_true, fn_false, operands)` as a rewrite inside a compiled region, which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Both are compiler-friendly under torch.compile: `torch.where` is expressible in Inductor as pointwise select; `torch.cond` is captured as a control-flow op and preserved through torch.export as well.
Only `torch.cond` preserves the correct data-dependent semantics; `torch.where` is semantically incorrect for any data-dependent selection and should never be used to replace an `if` branch.
`torch.where` evaluates both branches (elementwise or shape-compatible tensors) and selects per element; it is a good rewrite when both arms are cheap and produce compatible-shape outputs.
`torch.cond` captures each arm as a subgraph (only one arm runs at runtime), which is preferable when arms are expensive or have side effects that should not both execute.

explanation: A: `torch.where` computes both arms and selects per element — appropriate when both arms are cheap. B: `torch.cond` captures each arm as a subgraph and only one runs at execution time — appropriate when arms are expensive or have differing side effects. D: both are compile-friendly (Inductor lowers `torch.where` to a pointwise select; `torch.cond` is preserved as a control-flow op). C is wrong: `torch.where` is a valid, semantically-correct selection when both arms produce shape-compatible outputs; it evaluates eagerly but selects per element with the same semantics as a data-parallel if.

optionExplanations.B: Wrong: torch.where has correct selection semantics.

assumptions: PyTorch 2.3 ~ 2.5 with torch.cond support in the export IR.
The two arms produce shape-compatible outputs.
nonImplications: Does not imply `torch.cond` is always faster than `torch.where`; runtime cost depends on arm cost and hardware.
Does not imply that using `torch.cond` avoids all specialization; other guards can still fire.
